l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), 5 / RQ2: Can retrieval data affect the / 5.1 / Evaluation setup .. 5.4 / Discussions & Practical Implications
s: This unit examines whether retrieval data affects the memorization and reproduction of training-set information by large language models in retrieval-augmented generation. Using GPT-Neo-1.3B and Enron_Mail examples, the study compares targeted and prefix attacks with no retrieval, noise or prompts, and several retrieval datasets. Retrieval data substantially reduces extraction of personal identifying information and reconstruction of memorized text, although W3C-Email retrieval data leads the model to output more retrieval data instead of training data. The authors suggest that retrieval shifts generation toward the retrieved context and may reduce privacy leakage from training data while creating risks for information extraction from retrieval data itself.

l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), 6 / Conclusions
s: The paper investigates privacy risks associated with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large language models (LLMs). It evaluates retrieval data extraction using proposed attack methods and explores defense techniques that can mitigate these risks. The paper finds that integrating retrieval data can substantially reduce LLMs’ tendency to output memorized training data, suggesting that RAG could help mitigate training data leakage. These findings provide insights into privacy concerns relevant to the use of retrieval-augmented LLMs in real-world applications.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Abstract
s: The unit concerns Generative AI systems and their propensity to hallucinate, especially in real-world deployments. It describes an enterprise application that generates workflows from natural language requirements using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system uses RAG to improve the quality of structured workflow output, reduce hallucination, and generalize to out-of-domain settings. It also shows that a small, well-trained retriever can allow a smaller accompanying Large Language Model without reducing performance.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: The unit concerns using Large Language Models and Generative AI to convert natural language requirements into executable workflows represented as structured JSON documents. It explains that workflows can improve employee productivity but require specialized knowledge, which GenAI may help reduce for novice users. The text describes Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a method for reducing hallucination and improving workflow-generation quality, especially when enterprise-specific steps or database tables are involved. It reports that RAG can enable a smaller LLM and a very small retriever model to perform without loss in performance.

l: Large Language Models, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Large Language Models support structured output tasks such as converting natural language to code, SQL, and workflows. The text states that sufficiently large models can produce reasonably good workflows but may hallucinate, particularly for out-of-distribution inputs.

l: structured output tasks, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Structured output tasks include converting natural language into code, SQL, or workflows. The unit presents workflow generation as an application of this task type.

l: natural language to workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Natural language to workflows involves translating a natural language requirement into a series of steps and logic elements that specify their relationships. The unit describes using RAG to improve the trustworthiness of this translation.

l: workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Workflows are processes consisting of steps and logic elements that are executed automatically under certain conditions. They can increase employee productivity and standardize repetitive processes, but creating them requires specialized knowledge.

l: Generative AI, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Generative AI can lower the barrier to workflow creation by allowing novice users to describe desired workflow behavior in natural language. The text cautions that naive use of LLMs can produce untrustworthy outputs.

l: hallucination, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Hallucination in workflow generation means producing properties such as steps or database tables that do not exist. The unit identifies reducing hallucination as a central reason for using Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is used to reduce hallucination and improve the quality and trustworthiness of generated workflows. The text reports that it can support enterprise customization and allow a smaller LLM to perform without loss in performance.

l: JSON, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: JSON is used as the structured output format for generated workflows. Each workflow step is represented as a JSON object.

l: JSON output document, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: JSON documents represent workflows, including workflow steps and properties that identify relationships between steps. They may also include a trigger step and, in some cases, a database table name required by that trigger.

l: workflow generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Workflow generation converts natural language requirements into structured workflow outputs. The unit presents RAG for workflow generation and states that it reduces hallucination and improves results.

l: fine-tuning, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: Fine-tuning a sufficiently large LLM can produce reasonably good workflows, but fine-tuning separately for each enterprise may be prohibitively expensive because of infrastructure costs.

l: commercial GenAI application, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: A commercial GenAI application for workflow creation needs to minimize the mismatch caused by enterprise users adding customized workflow steps. The unit describes RAG as a way to address this need without fine-tuning an LLM for every enterprise.

l: retriever, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 1
s: A very small retriever model can be used with RAG in workflow generation. The text states that this combination allows deployment of a smaller LLM without loss in performance.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The unit explains how Retrieval-Augmented Generation is adapted from retrieving factual information to retrieving JSON objects for structured output generation. It describes the role of the retriever, emphasizing Dense Retrieval and training similar to Structure Aware DeNse ReTrievAl (SANTA) for aligning natural language queries with structured documents. It discusses challenges in structured output tasks, including valid parsing and selecting entities or field values from large, customizable vocabularies. It also contrasts Code LLMs and Guided Generation with the proposed retrieval-based approach, noting that grammar constraints alone do not provide knowledge about which workflow steps to include.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is commonly used to reduce false or outdated information by retrieving relevant information before text generation. In this work, it is adapted for structured output by retrieving JSON objects that could form part of the generated document.

l: JSON objects, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: JSON objects are retrieved as candidate components of a JSON output document. Providing plausible JSON objects to the LLM increases the likelihood that the output properties exist and that the generated JSON can be executed.

l: JSON output document, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The JSON output document is generated from retrieved JSON objects rather than only retrieved factual information. Its validity and executability are important goals of the approach.

l: Large Language Models, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The LLM receives retrieved JSON objects before generation and uses them to generate structured JSON output. The unit also notes that an LLM can be guided by a grammar, although grammar constraints do not provide knowledge about which workflow steps should be included.

l: retriever, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The retriever is a crucial component of Retrieval-Augmented Generation because its output becomes part of the LLM input. In this work, it retrieves structured JSON objects for unstructured natural-language queries.

l: Dense Retrieval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Dense Retrieval represents queries and documents in a multidimensional semantic space. The unit describes it as more effective than lexical methods such as TF-IDF or BM25 in many retrieval settings.

l: Structure Aware DeNse ReTrievAl (SANTA), Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The retrieval training in this work is described as similar to Structure Aware DeNse ReTrievAl (SANTA). SANTA proposes a method for aligning the semantics of code and text.

l: structured output tasks, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Structured output tasks generate valid structured data from natural language, including text-to-code, text-to-SQL, and if-then program synthesis. They require both parseable output and entities or field values that exist in a given lexicon.

l: natural language, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Natural language is used as the unstructured form of the query. In the described retrieval setting, it is matched against structured JSON objects.

l: pool of steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The pool of steps contains the steps that can be included in a workflow. It may be very large and customizable for each deployment, making it impractical to provide the entire pool through in-context learning.

l: workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The workflow is represented using a domain-specific JSON schema and consists of steps selected in response to a natural-language query. The unit states that grammar-based generation does not determine which steps the workflow should include.

l: LLMs, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: LLMs have made structured output tasks more accessible. Fine-tuning them on a small dataset can improve result quality, but additional measures are needed to reduce hallucination and support out-of-domain queries.

l: Code LLMs, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Code LLMs help developers generate code snippets from instructions and are trained on large datasets of source code. They have broad knowledge of programming languages and perform better on tasks requiring reasoning, but they cannot be used off-the-shelf for the domain-specific workflow JSON schema.

l: JSON schema, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The JSON schema used to represent workflows is domain-specific. Because of this, Code LLMs require adaptation rather than off-the-shelf use.

l: Guided Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: Guided Generation uses tools such as Outlines to constrain LLM output with a sufficiently expressive context-free grammar. It can ensure that generated steps exist, but it does not supply knowledge about which steps should be selected for a natural-language query.

l: user query, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2
s: The user query is used by both the retriever and the LLM in the high-level architecture. It provides the natural-language input for retrieving relevant JSON objects and generating the structured JSON output.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The RAG system retrieves relevant workflow steps and database tables, appends them to a user query, and prompts an LLM to generate a workflow in JSON format using greedy decoding. The retriever is fine-tuned to align natural-language requirements with structured step and table JSON objects, using positive and negative training pairs with contrastive loss. The LLM is trained separately through standard supervised fine-tuning on prompts augmented with retriever suggestions, assuming the required items are present in those suggestions. FAISS indexes the steps and tables for cosine-similarity retrieval at inference time.

l: RAG system, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The RAG system creates indices of steps and tables during initialization. For each user request, it retrieves suggestions, appends them to the query, and uses an LLM to generate a workflow in JSON format.

l: retriever, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The retriever maps natural-language queries to existing step and database table names. It is fine-tuned on query-to-step or query-to-table pairs, uses negative sampling, and retrieves the maximum K steps and tables associated with a requirement.

l: LLM, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The LLM receives the user query together with suggested steps and tables in JSON format. It is trained to generate the workflow as structured JSON, using greedy decoding during generation.

l: workflow, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The workflow is generated from a user request and consists of related steps represented in structured JSON. Its required steps and, when applicable, table names are included among the retriever suggestions during LLM training.

l: user query, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The user query is embedded by the retriever and used to retrieve relevant steps and tables. It is then combined with those suggestions to form the LLM prompt.

l: steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Steps are indexed and retrieved as possible components of a workflow. The retriever is trained to map queries to existing step names because step names are a major source of potential hallucination.

l: database table, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Database tables are indexed and retrieved when a trigger step requires a table name. A query can map to zero tables when its workflow does not require one.

l: JSON output document, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: JSON objects represent steps or tables for retriever training and retrieval. The LLM is given relevant JSON objects in its prompt so it can copy them during structured output generation.

l: retriever encoder, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The retriever encoder is fine-tuned to align natural language with structured JSON objects and to represent application-specific terminology. It produces normalized fixed-length vectors for user queries, steps, and tables.

l: siamese transformer encoder, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: The siamese transformer encoder encodes user queries and step or table JSON objects using mean pooling. A normalization layer produces embeddings with norm 1.

l: embedding, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Embeddings are generated for user queries, steps, and tables by the retriever. Their cosine similarity is used to retrieve the steps and tables most associated with a requirement.

l: contrastive loss, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Contrastive loss trains the retriever to minimize the distance between positive query-object pairs and separate negative pairs. It uses cosine distance and a margin of one half for negative examples.

l: FAISS, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: FAISS is used during initialization to build indices of steps and tables. Those indices support retrieval after an incoming query has been embedded.

l: cosine similarity, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Cosine similarity is calculated between the query embedding and step or table embeddings. The retriever uses it to select the maximum K relevant steps and tables.

l: standard LLM supervised fine-tuning, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Standard LLM supervised fine-tuning is performed after the retriever augments the dataset with suggested step and table names. The training examples use short prompts and expected workflow JSON outputs.

l: retrieval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Retrieval supplies suggested steps and tables for a natural-language requirement. During LLM training, the system assumes retrieval has 100% recall for the required items, except for the most frequent steps that are expected to be memorized.

l: fine-tuning, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3 .. 3.2
s: Training first fine-tunes the retriever on positive and sampled negative query-object pairs. The LLM is then trained separately on prompts augmented with retriever outputs and workflow JSON targets.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: The experiments concern a commercial enterprise system that generates workflow JSON documents from natural language requirements using an LLM and a RAG system. The authors create in-domain, Human Eval, and out-of-domain datasets from deployed workflows, user interactions, and deterministic samples, and evaluate them with workflow-generation and retrieval metrics. They fine-tune StarCoderBase variants and compare CodeLlama-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.1, while also comparing retriever encoders. The Human Eval split is used for the final metrics because it provides more realistic and higher-quality inputs than the Test split.

l: commercial enterprise system, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: The commercial enterprise system is the production context for the workflow-generation task. Its deployments provide workflow examples and motivate constraints on model and retriever size.

l: workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: Workflows are extracted from internal deployments, generated deterministically in simple incremental-building cases, and collected from other enterprise-platform deployments for out-of-domain evaluation. They are represented by expected JSON documents containing triggers, steps, and sometimes tables.

l: user query, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: Natural language requirements are written by annotators for deployed workflows and entered by expert users during simulated system interactions. They are used as inputs for workflow generation and retrieval evaluation.

l: JSON output document, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: JSON documents represent the expected workflows and contain triggers, steps, and, when required, tables. They are used as ground truth for evaluating generation and retriever coverage.

l: Human Eval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: Human Eval is an additional dataset split created from expert users simulating interactions with the system through a simple user interface. The final metrics use this 157-example split instead of the Test split because its inputs are higher quality and more realistic.

l: Train split, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: The Train split contains 2,867 in-domain examples, including 823 triggers and 556 tables. It is also part of the source data used to create retriever training pairs, and its set of steps is used to measure how different the out-of-domain splits are.

l: Test split, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: The Test split contains 798 in-domain examples, including 247 triggers and 163 tables. It is not used for the final metrics because Human Eval is considered higher quality and more realistic.

l: out-of-domain splits, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 / 4.1 .. 4.3
s: The out-of-domain splits consist of five sets of real workflows from other enterprise-platform deployments. Their shares of steps absent from the Train split range from 7% to 76%, demonstrating variation from the training data and the need for retrieval and deployment-specific indices.

s: The unit evaluates retriever encoders, retrieval-augmented generation, and StarCoderBase models for workflow generation on the Human Eval and OOD splits. Error analysis identifies retriever omissions and failures to generate structures involving IF, TRY, and FOREACH as important issues, while engineering analysis favors modular deployment of the retriever and LLM.

s: The retriever encoder shows limited improvement when scaled as an off-the-shelf encoder, but fine-tuning substantially improves retrieval. The system uses a fine-tuned 110M-parameter encoder for deployment, and its small size permits deployment on the same GPU as the LLM or on CPU.

s: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces hallucinated steps and tables while preserving overall workflow-generation performance. s: The LLM generates structured workflow documents using retrieved step and table suggestions. Larger LLMs copy and paste retrieved content more effectively, but the LLM can fail to produce the desired structure, especially for IF, TRY, and FOREACH steps.

s: Fine-tuning is crucial for improving the retriever, whereas scaling off-the-shelf encoders does not yield significant retrieval gains. Fine-tuning the LLM with RAG reduces hallucination, and all evaluated models produce valid JSON documents following the expected schema.

s: Hallucination is measured separately for steps and tables, with lower values being better. A retriever reduces hallucinated steps to below 7.5% and hallucinated tables to below 4.5% for the StarCoderBase models, although tables hallucinate more when suggestions are removed.

s: The generated workflow must follow the expected JSON schema and contain steps and tables consistent with the user query. Workflow failures arise when retrieval omits crucial components or when the LLM does not generate the desired structure for logic-related steps.

s: OOD evaluation measures the RAG fine-tuned StarCoderBase-7B on five out-of-distribution splits without additional retriever or LLM fine-tuning. Its weighted average results are similar to the Human Eval results across Trigger EM, Bag of Steps, hallucinated steps, and hallucinated tables.

s: Trigger Exact Match evaluates whether the generated workflow matches the expected trigger. With RAG, larger StarCoderBase models generally perform better, and StarCoderBase-7B achieves 0.664 on Human Eval and 0.647 on the weighted OOD average.

s: Bag of Steps measures the generated step set without focusing on ordering. RAG improves or maintains this metric across models and OOD splits, with StarCoderBase-7B achieving 0.672 on Human Eval and 0.714 on the weighted OOD average.

l: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Abstract
s: The text introduces DRAGIN, a framework for dynamic retrieval augmented generation based on the information needs of Large Language Models (LLMs). It addresses when to activate the retrieval module and what query to use during text generation. Unlike existing methods that rely on static rules and recent text, DRAGIN considers information needs across the entire context. Experiments on four knowledge-intensive generation datasets show that DRAGIN achieves superior performance on all tasks.

l: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: The unit concerns large language models (LLMs), their tendency to produce factually incorrect but plausible text, and retrieval-based methods for mitigating this problem. It explains that traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation uses single-round retrieval, while dynamic RAG retrieves multiple times during generation by deciding when and what to retrieve. The authors introduce DRAGIN, a lightweight framework that uses Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND) to determine when retrieval is needed and Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS) to determine what to retrieve. Experiments on four knowledge-intensive generation benchmarks show that DRAGIN outperforms existing dynamic RAG frameworks and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

l: large language models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Large language models have advanced across many natural language processing tasks and have become important in numerous AI applications. They can generate coherent and plausible text that is factually incorrect, and DRAGIN is designed to augment them dynamically without further training, fine-tuning, or prompt engineering.

l: hallucination, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Hallucination refers to the production of text by large language models that appears coherent and plausible but is factually incorrect. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is presented as a prominent approach for mitigating this problem.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances large language models by retrieving relevant information from external databases and incorporating it into their inputs. Traditional methods generally use single-round retrieval based on the initial input and may be less effective for complex multi-step and long-form generation tasks.

l: dynamic RAG, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Dynamic RAG performs retrieval multiple times during language-model generation. It requires decisions about when retrieval should be activated and what query should be used, but existing approaches often rely on static timing rules and recent sentences or tokens, which can cause unnecessary retrieval, add noise and cost, or miss the model's broader information needs.

l: DRAGIN, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: DRAGIN is a dynamic retrieval-augmented generation framework based on the information needs of large language models. It uses Real-time Information Needs Detection to decide when to retrieve and Query Formulation based on Self-attention to formulate queries from the entire context, and it achieves superior performance on four knowledge-intensive generation benchmarks.

l: Real-time Information Needs Detection, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Real-time Information Needs Detection is DRAGIN's strategy for deciding when to retrieve. It considers the language model's uncertainty about generated content, each token's influence on subsequent tokens, and each token's semantic significance.

l: Query Formulation based on Self-attention, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Query Formulation based on Self-attention is DRAGIN's strategy for deciding what to retrieve. It formulates queries by using the language model's self-attention across the entire context rather than restricting the query to only the most recent sentence or a few tokens.

l: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: This unit reviews single-round and multi-round retrieval-augmented methods for large language models. Single-round retrieval augmentation uses the initial input to retrieve external information, while multi-round methods retrieve information during generation for complex tasks. It discusses methods including REPLUG, UniWeb, RETRO, ICRALM, IRCot, and FLARE, noting the limitations of fixed-interval or uncertainty-based retrieval. The unit also illustrates the DRAGIN framework, which detects information needs during generation and formulates retrieval queries, using an Einstein example.

l: large language models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: Large language models are effective across many tasks but can fall short on knowledge-intensive tasks. Retrieval augmentation is used to provide them with information from external corpora.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation strategies enhance large language models by incorporating retrieved external knowledge into the model input.

l: single-round retrieval augmentation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: Single-round retrieval augmentation uses the initial user input as a query to retrieve information from an external corpus, then incorporates the retrieved knowledge into the model input. It can be relatively effective for simple tasks or clear-cut information needs, but may not provide all the knowledge required for complex or lengthy tasks.

l: multi-round retrieval augmentation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: Multi-round retrieval augmentation retrieves information during generation and is explored for complex tasks such as long-form question answering, multi-hop reasoning, and chain-of-thought reasoning. RETRO and ICRALM trigger retrieval at fixed token intervals, IRCot triggers it every sentence, and FLARE triggers it when a generated token has a probability below a threshold.

l: external knowledge, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: External knowledge is retrieved from a corpus and incorporated into the input or generation process of a large language model. In the Einstein example, retrieved passages provide different claims about the job Einstein secured in 1903.

l: DRAGIN, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: DRAGIN is illustrated as a framework for continual generation based on external knowledge. Its components include RIND, which detects real-time information needs, and QFS, which formulates retrieval queries based on self-attention.

l: Einstein, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.2
s: Einstein is used in an example request for a brief introduction. The retrieved passages state that he was born in the German Empire, moved to Switzerland in 1895, and secured a job in 1903, with the passages differing on whether this was at the University of Zurich or the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.

l: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: The unit introduces DRAGIN, a dynamic RAG framework consisting of Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND) and Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS). RIND determines when retrieval is needed by combining token entropy, maximum attention from following tokens, and a binary semantic indicator for stopwords. QFS formulates retrieval queries by selecting the highest-attended preceding tokens at the detected position. After retrieval, the language model truncates its output, incorporates retrieved documents through a prompt, and continues generation, repeating the process when another information need is detected.

l: DRAGIN, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: DRAGIN is a dynamic RAG framework with two components: Real-time Information Needs Detection and Query Formulation based on Self-attention. It detects information needs during generation, formulates queries, retrieves external knowledge, and continues generation using that knowledge.

l: Real-time Information Needs Detection, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: Real-time Information Needs Detection identifies when retrieval should be activated by evaluating token uncertainty, semantic contribution, and influence on subsequent context. It computes a score by multiplying token entropy, maximum following-token attention, and a binary indicator that filters stopwords, and triggers retrieval when the score exceeds a threshold.

l: Query Formulation based on Self-attention, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: Query Formulation based on Self-attention creates a retrieval query at the position identified by Real-time Information Needs Detection. It selects the top attended preceding tokens, restores their original order, and uses the corresponding words to construct the query.

l: dynamic RAG, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: Dynamic RAG frameworks trigger retrieval during language-model generation. In DRAGIN, retrieval is activated using a token-level information-need score, and the process can be repeated at later positions with newly retrieved documents.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: Retrieval-augmented generation integrates external knowledge into continued language-model generation. In this unit, the output is truncated at the detected position, retrieved documents are added to a prompt, and generation resumes from the truncated output.

l: large language models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: The large language model generates tokens while recording token probabilities and last-layer attention scores. After retrieval, it receives a prompt containing external knowledge and the truncated answer, then continues generating.

l: self-attention, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: Self-attention is used to measure token influence and formulate queries. Attention from following tokens helps determine whether retrieval is needed, while attention assigned to preceding tokens identifies the context words most relevant to the next generated token.

s: A token is evaluated using its vocabulary-distribution entropy, its maximum attention from subsequent tokens, and a semantic indicator that excludes stopwords. A token whose combined score exceeds the predefined threshold causes retrieval to activate.

s: Attention values are computed from query and key vectors using a scaled dot product followed by softmax. The unit uses attention scores from the last Transformer layer to measure token influence and select query terms.

l: retrieval models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: The retrieval model uses the query produced by Query Formulation based on Self-attention to retrieve relevant information from external knowledge bases. An off-the-shelf model such as BM25 can serve this role.

s: Retrieved documents are inserted into a prompt as external knowledge references. Three documents are illustrated at each retrieval step, and a later retrieval event can replace them with a newly retrieved set.

l: real-time information needs, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: An information need is detected when a token's combined uncertainty, attention influence, and semantic score exceeds the threshold. The detected position determines when retrieval occurs and where the generated output is truncated.

l: external knowledge, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models, 3 .. 3.3
s: External knowledge is retrieved from knowledge bases and presented to the language model as numbered references. It is used to support the continuation of generation after the output has been truncated.

s: Generation proceeds token by token until an information need triggers retrieval. After retrieved knowledge is integrated, generation resumes from the truncation point and may trigger further retrieval at a subsequent position.

s: The unit describes experiments evaluating DRAGIN and other retrieval-augmented generation methods on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, IIRC, and StrategyQA. s: DRAGIN is evaluated for multihop reasoning, reading comprehension, and commonsense reasoning against other retrieval-augmented generation methods.
